Question: Can agents operate at configurable autonomy tiers (fully supervised to fully autonomous)? Does autonomy adjust based on task risk, confidence score, and historical success rate?
Response: Yes. Autonomy is deterministic by default, agentic by exception: thresholds are configuration values enforced at two structural points in the MAF workflow graph. (1) A MAF validator executor downstream of an agent executor reads the typed confidence/risk fields on the agent's output and routes via conditional edges — auto-shortlist, exception queue or auto-reject — which is a deterministic code decision, not an LLM decision. (2) A GHCP SDK session hook inside the agent executor enforces per-tool autonomy boundaries (non-revocable actions intercepted regardless of confidence). Example (POC2 screening): confidence >85% → auto-shortlist edge; 60-85% → exception edge to HR BP; <60% → auto-reject edge. Thresholds adjust based on: task risk, confidence score, historical success rate (Fleet Manager analyses override patterns and proposes threshold or graph changes). Changes are audit-logged with operator identity, timestamp and rationale; governance changes flow via PR review (APIOps), not instant-apply sliders on safety-critical parameters. Autonomy dial UI writes to the config store read by the validator executor.
Key Technologies: Configurable thresholds (runtime-adjustable), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) validator executors (deterministic routing), GHCP SDK hooks (enforcement), Fleet Manager (threshold proposals), Control Plane UI (autonomy dials), APIOps PR review
POC Demo: POC2: Show autonomy dials on Control Plane — adjust screening auto-shortlist threshold from 85% to 75%, show immediate effect on next screening phase. Show audit trail of the change.

Question: Describe the formal process for moving workflows from experimental (generative) to standardised (deterministic): observation, statistical validation, code generation, review, promotion, monitoring.
Response: The crystallisation pipeline is expressed structurally as a migration inside the MAF workflow graph: agent executor node → deterministic plain-function executor node, with the agent executor preserved on a low-confidence fallback edge. Formal progression: (1) Observation: the agent executor runs generatively; MAF workflow spans plus GHCP SDK session OTEL capture the execution. A MAF validator executor downstream asserts schema/policy. (2) Statistical validation: after N successful runs where the validator passes and Fleet Manager sees low override rates, a crystallisation candidate is proposed. (3) Code generation: consistent patterns are extracted into deterministic code by an agentic builder or a developer. (4) Review: human reviews via Control Plane or PR. (5) Promotion: skill registered in Azure API Center; the MAF workflow graph is updated to swap the agent node for the plain-function node on the happy path; APIOps CI/CD promotes Design → Preview → Production with approval gates. (6) Monitoring: the deterministic executor runs in production; Foundry Evaluators compare quality against the generative baseline; validator executor failure rate is a drift signal. If quality degrades, Fleet Manager alerts. Fallback: on low confidence or validator failure, the graph conditional edge routes to the preserved agent executor.
Key Technologies: Skill crystallisation pipeline, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph (agent → plain-function executor migration), Azure API Center lifecycle, APIOps CI/CD, Foundry Evaluators, Fleet Manager monitoring, OTEL observation

Question: Can crystallised workflows invoke generative orchestration when encountering novel exceptions? Are exceptions logged, analysed, and fed into new crystallisation cycles?
Response: Yes. Fallback is expressed as a conditional edge in the MAF workflow graph: when the deterministic plain-function executor encounters input it cannot process (novel CV format, unexpected invoice structure) or a downstream validator executor rejects its output, the graph routes to the preserved agent executor (GHCP SDK session) with full generative capability — the LLM reasons about the novel situation with all available context, wrapped by pre/post hooks and Foundry Guardrails. The exception is: (1) Logged with full context via OTEL; (2) Analysed by the Fleet Manager — one-off anomaly or pattern? (3) Fed into the next crystallisation cycle — if similar exceptions recur, the deterministic executor is updated or a new plain-function executor is added. Durable Functions coordinates across phases and replays any orchestration-level failures. The entire cycle is visible on the Control Plane.
Key Technologies: MAF workflow graph (conditional fallback edge: plain-function ↔ agent executor), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) validator executors, Azure Durable Functions, GHCP SDK hooks + Foundry Guardrails, Fleet Manager (pattern analysis), Control Plane (visibility)
POC Demo: POC2: Show crystallised CV parser encountering novel format — fallback to generative, successful processing, exception logged for next crystallisation cycle.

Question: Describe policy-as-code enforcement across the full agent lifecycle. Are policies: version-controlled, adaptive (runtime context), composable (inheritance), audit-trailed, and testable (dry-run against historical traces)?
Response: Governance-as-code operates across multiple layers, all Git-committed and version-controlled. (1) Version-controlled: APIM policies via APIOps CI/CD, GHCP SDK hooks in Git, MAF workflow graph definitions and validator executors in Git, Foundry Guardrails config per agent, jurisdiction-specific skills as SKILL.md files, autonomy thresholds in config store with change tracking. (2) Adaptive: policies adapt to runtime context — jurisdiction-specific skills load based on workflow context, APIM routes based on jurisdiction metadata, autonomy thresholds are per-workflow adjustable. (3) Composable: skills inherit base governance from their domain (all hiring skills inherit GDPR rules), jurisdiction-specific rules layer on top (German hires add works council notifications). APIM policies compose with inheritance. MAF workflow graphs compose — a reusable compliance sub-graph (validator chain) can be wired into any phase. (4) Audit-trailed: every policy change logged with author, timestamp, rationale. Every enforcement decision logged via OTEL, APIM and MAF validator span events. (5) Testable: policies evaluated against historical traces via Foundry Evaluators and MAF graph replay — "if we change this threshold or add this validator, how many past cases would have been affected?" Policy dry-run before deployment. (6) Data classification: policies enforce the 4-class data model (Workflow state in Cosmos with CMK and region-pinning, Model context ephemeral and Guardrails-redacted, Audit ledger immutable 7-12y in Log Analytics, Telemetry in App Insights without prompt bodies) — reasoning chain separated from action ledger. (7) Residency-as-code: APIOps CI gate rejects PRs that register cross-region backends against jurisdiction-tagged skills (e.g. a DE-tagged skill cannot point to a US model endpoint) — residency is an enforced boundary, not a runtime hope.
Key Technologies: APIOps CI/CD, GHCP SDK hooks, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graphs & validator executors (governance-as-code), Foundry Guardrails, jurisdiction skills, Foundry Evaluators (dry-run), OTEL audit
